headline: Dry sunshine and chilly nights dominate through Tuesday; Kentucky frost and valley fog tonight give way to a warmer start to the week before a later Wednesday weather change
disclaimer: Independent amateur analysis. This is not an official forecast or warning. Follow the National Weather Service and local authorities during hazardous weather.

refresh.workflow: Update and commit forecast.json once. GitHub Actions automatically locks the prior issue in forecast-history.json. Then verify the GitHub Pages URL; every Google Sites embed reads the same file and refreshes automatically.

kentucky.name: Central Kentucky
kentucky.subtitle: Danville primary · Lexington comparison
kentucky.summary: Dry high pressure and a very dry column control Central Kentucky through Tuesday. Clear sky and light wind allow strong radiational cooling tonight, producing widespread frost and patchy river-valley fog under an official Frost Advisory. West to southwest flow then brings a gradual daytime warm-up Monday and Tuesday. By early Wednesday, the polar and subtropical jets begin interacting and low pressure starts organizing, but current point guidance keeps the area dry through the afternoon endpoint; meaningful rain and stronger wind are favored after this forecast expires.
kentucky.currentConditions: At 2:55 PM EST, KDVK reported 59°F with a 36°F dew point, southwest wind near 7 mph, visibility above 10 miles and clear sky. At 2:54 PM, KLEX reported 59°F with a 36°F dew point, southwest wind near 12 mph, visibility above 10 miles and clear sky. An official NWS Frost Advisory includes Boyle and Fayette Counties from midnight tonight through 10:00 AM Monday.

days.label: Sunday
days.hazard: OFFICIAL NWS FROST ADVISORY: Boyle County is included from midnight tonight through 10:00 AM Monday; temperatures as low as 34°F are expected to produce frost. Independent analysis agrees that frost is likely. The most sheltered rural valleys may briefly reach freezing, and patchy river-valley fog is possible toward dawn, but a widespread hard freeze or dense-fog event is not expected.
days.forecast: The remainder of the afternoon stays sunny and dry, with a most-likely Danville high near 59°F. West wind runs about 5–10 mph with occasional gusts near 10–18 mph, then becomes light this evening. Clear sky, low dew points and diminishing wind support efficient radiational cooling tonight. The most-likely Danville low is near 34°F; the established KDVK cold correction and terrain effects support lower readings near 31–32°F in favored hollows. Frost becomes widespread late, while shallow valley fog may form mainly near waterways.

days.label: Monday
days.hazard: OFFICIAL NWS FROST ADVISORY remains in effect through 10:00 AM. After it expires, no official point alert covers Monday night. Independent concern is limited to patchy early frost and fog, followed by another localized frost risk late Monday night in the coldest valleys; widespread freezing conditions are not expected.
days.forecast: Patchy frost and river-valley fog dissipate after sunrise. Surface high pressure and dry west flow maintain full sunshine, allowing a most-likely Danville high near 63°F. Wind remains light, generally west at 4–8 mph with gusts below 15 mph. Monday night stays clear and chilly. The most-likely Danville low is near 36°F after the established local correction, while colder Bluegrass hollows may approach freezing. Any fog should remain shallow and localized.

days.label: Tuesday / early Wednesday
days.hazard: No official NWS point alert currently covers Tuesday or early Wednesday. No threshold wind, thunder or heavy-rain hazard is expected before the 72-hour endpoint. Low pressure organizes nearby Wednesday, but point guidance keeps meaningful rain, stronger wind and the later cold-air change beyond this forecast.
days.forecast: A weak southern-stream disturbance passes well to the south while dry southwest flow continues over the Bluegrass. Tuesday remains sunny with a most-likely Danville high near 66°F; southwest wind runs 5–10 mph with gusts generally below 18 mph. Tuesday night is mostly clear with a most-likely low near 40°F and only a small localized fog risk. Veterans Day begins dry and mostly sunny, then some clouds increase. Temperatures recover into the middle 60s by early afternoon. The point-guidance precipitation chance remains 5% or less through the endpoint; the later Wednesday rain and wind remain a watch item outside this forecast.

kentucky.bottomLine: Central Kentucky stays dry and sunny through Tuesday. The main near-term hazard is tonight’s official Frost Advisory, with a most-likely Danville low near 34°F and colder rural hollows near freezing. Most-likely highs are 59°F today, 63°F Monday and 66°F Tuesday. Wednesday begins dry and remains at 5% or less for rain through the early-afternoon endpoint; the more consequential rain, wind and cold change follow later.
kentucky.confidence: High on the dry forecast through Tuesday and tonight’s frost; high on daytime temperatures; moderate-high on exact overnight lows; moderate on localized fog; moderate on the arrival time of Wednesday’s first showers

upstate.name: Upstate South Carolina
upstate.subtitle: Clemson primary · Central/Pickens County comparison
upstate.summary: Dry high pressure remains over the Southeast through early Wednesday. Sunshine and very low rain chances accompany above-normal afternoon temperatures, while clear sky and light wind produce large day-to-night temperature swings. The Clemson–Central corridor remains warmer than the advised North Carolina foothills, although the coldest sheltered Pickens County pockets may see patchy grass frost. A few isolated valley-fog signals appear in high-resolution guidance, but broader profiles and official guidance do not support widespread fog.
upstate.currentConditions: At 2:55 PM EST, KLQK reported 70°F with a 45°F dew point, southwest wind near 9 mph, visibility above 10 miles and clear sky. At 2:54 PM, KCEU reported 70°F with a 46°F dew point, light variable wind, visibility above 10 miles and clear sky. No official NWS point alert was active for Clemson or Central at the final check. Tempest data was not used.

days.label: Sunday
days.hazard: No official NWS point alert is active for Clemson or Central. No threshold independent hazard is expected. The coldest sheltered locations near Central and Pickens may see patchy grass frost late tonight, and isolated river-valley fog is possible; a corridor-wide freeze or dense-fog event is not expected.
days.forecast: The remainder of the afternoon stays sunny and dry, with a most-likely high near 70°F. Southwest wind runs 3–8 mph with occasional gusts near 10–18 mph before becoming light or calm tonight. Clear sky and dry air support a chilly night. Applying the maintained station corrections gives most-likely lows near 41°F at Clemson and 36°F around Central/Pickens. Several KAND high-resolution profiles support brief near-dawn valley saturation, while KGSP and GFS do not; fog therefore remains conditional and localized.

days.label: Monday
days.hazard: No official NWS point alert is active. No threshold independent hazard is expected. Patchy frost is possible only in the coldest sheltered pockets near dawn, and a limited river-valley fog possibility returns late Monday night; neither is expected to become widespread across the Clemson–Central corridor.
days.forecast: Any isolated valley fog or patchy frost dissipates quickly, followed by full sunshine. Rising heights and dry high pressure support a most-likely afternoon high near 72°F. Wind is light northwest becoming variable, mainly 0–5 mph with gusts below 10 mph. Monday night remains clear with most-likely lows near 43°F at Clemson and 38°F around Central/Pickens after the verified station corrections. Local drainage pockets may be colder.

days.label: Tuesday / early Wednesday
days.hazard: No official NWS point alert currently covers Tuesday or early Wednesday. No threshold independent hazard is expected: rain and thunder remain unlikely, wind stays light, and freezing temperatures are not expected in the corridor.
days.forecast: Mostly sunny sky and dry high pressure continue Tuesday. Some thin high cloud may arrive late, but it should not prevent a most-likely high near 70°F. Wind remains light and variable, becoming southwest at 0–6 mph with gusts below 12 mph. Tuesday night stays dry with most-likely lows near 45°F at Clemson and 40°F around Central/Pickens. Veterans Day remains dry and mostly sunny through the early-afternoon endpoint, warming toward 71–72°F on light southwest to west wind.

upstate.bottomLine: The Upstate stays dry and mostly sunny through the full 72 hours. Most-likely highs are near 70°F today, 72°F Monday and 70°F Tuesday, with early Wednesday reaching the lower 70s. Bias-corrected nighttime centers are Clemson 41°F, 43°F and 45°F, and Central/Pickens 36°F, 38°F and 40°F. Only localized frost or valley fog is possible; no widespread freeze or rain is expected.
upstate.confidence: High on the dry pattern and today’s temperature; moderate-high on Monday and Tuesday highs; moderate-high on nighttime station values; moderate on isolated sheltered frost and valley fog

sourceNotes: OFFICIAL ALERTS: an NWS Frost Advisory includes Boyle County from midnight tonight through 10:00 AM Monday for temperatures as low as 34°F and frost formation. No active NWS point alert was found for Clemson or Central. Official alerts remain explicitly separate from SPC/WPC outlooks and this independent analysis.

The 19:40Z Louisville discussion expects clear sky, light wind, lows in the lower to middle 30s, frost and river-valley fog tonight; dry mid-60s Monday, upper-60s Tuesday and rain chances returning Wednesday afternoon. Its Wednesday system is moisture-limited initially, with more consequential weather later than this 72-hour endpoint.

The 18:51Z Greenville-Spartanburg discussion keeps dry high pressure in control through midweek. It expects highs about 5°F above normal, large diurnal ranges, chilly nights and patchy fog mainly in mountain valleys; South Carolina has no advisory.

Latest official observations showed clear sky and unrestricted visibility at KDVK, KLEX, KCEU and KLQK. KDVK was near 59°F and the Upstate stations were near 70°F, supporting full insolation and invalidating the coldest same-day model maxima. Tempest was excluded.

College of DuPage radar and visible/infrared satellite imagery showed both forecast regions dry and largely cloud-free. Surface analysis showed no nearby boundary in the Upstate, while 500-mb, 850-mb dewpoint and precipitable-water analyses showed dry northwest/confluent flow and a moisture-poor column supporting zero QPF through Tuesday.

Chris Bailey’s exact November 8 Kentucky Weather Center post, ‘Winter Weather Possible Late This Week,’ was consulted as accepted authoritative source material. Bailey describes seasonably chilly weather today, a milder start to the week, then a deep eastern trough and a Wednesday–Thursday low with rain and wind ahead and cold or snow behind. His first GFS graphic keeps Kentucky dry through about 21Z Wednesday. Details absent from the post or unreadable in its graphics were left unknown.

Central Kentucky observations, the official forecast, fresh BUFKIT and validated GRIB guidance support a dry 59/63/66°F most-likely high sequence. Monday’s official 63°F and Tuesday’s 66°F are 2–4°F warmer than parts of the raw model cluster, but observed full sun, official local expertise and the complete multi-model envelope support those centers without requiring wider ranges.

Tonight’s official 34°F low is 1–4°F colder than several raw short-range profiles. Clear sky, light wind, the NWS frost headline, drainage terrain and the established KDVK −2°F correction justify the 34°F most-likely value. Calibrated card ranges preserve colder hollows and warmer urban exposure.

Monday-night KDVK guidance splits from roughly 38–39°F in HRRR/RAP and 37–39°F in RRFS proxy profiles to 42–43°F in the coarser globals. The official 36°F forecast, known drainage cooling and the −2°F KDVK correction favor the colder local branch; the calibrated 34–42°F card retains nearly all of the warmer branch without treating coarse-grid guidance as an exact valley forecast.

The first Wednesday precipitation signal remains beyond the 72-hour boundary. Updated NWS hourly, GFS, ECMWF and NBM point guidance hold at 0% through 1 PM and no higher than 5% by the early-afternoon endpoint; WPC 72-hour QPF has no measurable Danville amount through 00Z Thursday. Stronger rain, wind and the later cold-air transition are explicitly outside this forecast window.

Upstate official/NBM, GFS/GEFS and observations favor highs near 70°F today, 72°F Monday and 70°F Tuesday. The RRFS/ECMWF cold same-day branch was overtaken by observed temperatures. Monday’s 68–69°F RRFS/ECMWF branch remains plausible but is outweighed by NWS, NBM, GFS and GEFS; the calibrated 69–74°F range covers it.

Upstate coarse global and GEFS overnight grids remain too warm in clear, calm drainage conditions near KLQK. Most-likely lows therefore use NWS/NBM plus the maintained KCEU +2°F and KLQK −3°F corrections. Ten-degree calibrated low ranges describe the Clemson-to-Central and terrain spread, not uncertainty at one exact sensor.

Fresh HRRR and RAP KAND profiles join RRFS in showing brief near-saturation toward Monday dawn, while KGSP and GFS profiles do not. This is translated to a 20% conditional river/low-valley fog probability, greatest near dawn, rather than a corridor-wide or dense-fog forecast. Monday-night fog remains 10–15%.

SPC Days 1–3 contain no severe-thunderstorm area for either forecast region. WPC Days 1–2 place excessive-rainfall risk in Texas and Day 3 is below 5% nationwide. These national outlooks are not point alerts.
The locally extracted Central Kentucky GRIB package was generated at 2026-11-08T20:26:26Z. Every model is used only within its validated horizon; partial HRRR/RAP periods are not extrapolated.
Local GRIB disclosure: hrrr: hrrr ends at 2026-11-10T18:00Z and is partial-horizon guidance for this 72.0-hour window.
Local GRIB disclosure: rap: rap ends at 2026-11-10T18:00Z and is partial-horizon guidance for this 72.0-hour window.

The active BUFKIT 19 installation was refreshed with GFS 06Z, HRRR 17Z, RAP 18Z and operational RRFS 12Z profiles. KLEX/KSME bracket Danville; KAND/KGSP are regional Upstate proxies rather than exact KCEU/KLQK profiles.

NAM and NAM 3-km operational production ended after the 12Z November 3 cycle under NWS Service Change Notice 26-47. Retained cycles are stale and were excluded; RRFS is explicitly identified as the operational replacement and given a limited supplemental share until local verification samples accumulate.
The latest cumulative accuracy summary contains 127 verified of 135 checkpoints and all-category accuracy of 80% overall, including 83.6% for Central Kentucky and 76.3% for the Upstate.

Current station corrections, empirical lead-specific temperature widths, documented dry-high-pressure model weights, explicit fog/frost/rain timing and official-alert separation were applied. KDVK high remains monitoring with no adjustment; low corrections applied are KDVK −2°F, KCEU +2°F and KLQK −3°F.

Temperature cards use the current calibrated regional widths: Kentucky high/low widths of 5/9°F, 5/8°F and 7/8°F; Upstate widths of 4/10°F, 5/10°F and 6/10°F. Prose gives narrower most-likely station values.
All local times use Eastern Standard Time. The third card explicitly covers Tuesday night and early Wednesday because validThrough is exactly 72 elapsed hours after an afternoon issuance.
